newsitem.title: UK: UK to channel lottery funds to health, education.
newsitem.headline: UK to channel lottery funds to health, education.

text.p: The British government unveiled plans on Monday to pump one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) of national lottery money into projects to improve health, education and the environment.
"This will mark a turning point in the fortunes of our national lottery," Culture Secretary Chris Smith told a news conference, outlining plans to create what he called a "people's lottery".
The Labour government proposals, which will be followed by legislation later this year, come in the wake of controversy over profit and salary levels at national lottery operator Camelot.

The government said returns to the lottery operator and its directors must be "reasonable, related to performance and easily understood". It sought proposals on how to maximise funds for good causes such as charities, sports and the arts while removing "unnecessary" profit margins.

Smith denied that the government, which won a landslide victory in the election in May, was reneging on promises to transfer the lottery to a non-profit operator when Camelot's seven-year licence expires in 2001.
"The absolute priority has to be making sure we maximise the return for good causes," Smith said. "...The open-ended profit mechanism as we have at the moment does not maximise returns," he added.

He said he would welcome bids to run the licence after 2001 from Camelot and entrepreneur Richard Branson's Virgin Group. Branson put forward plans to run the lottery on a non-profit basis but lost out to Camelot in the original licence award.
Camelot, a five-company consortium, welcomed the review, saying it was pleased that the government had recognised its efficiency in raising money.

Some 30 million Britons play the lottery each week, lured by the prospect of winning millions for a one pound stake in a televised draw. Its popularity has led to the introduction of a second weekly draw and "scratchcards" offering instant cash prizes.

The lottery has so far raised more than 3.6 billion pounds for good causes. The government said it should raise at least 10 billion pounds by 2001, one billion pounds above forecast, and it wants to channel this extra funding into health, education and the environment.

Initial plans include measures to train teachers in the use of information technology, after-school activity clubs for children and a network of centres to promote healthy living. The government is also planning to set up a trust to foster the development of creative talent. ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
